newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba's 1996/97 sugar crop passes first mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Cuba's 1996/97 sugar crop passes first mln tonnes.

text.p: Cuba has produced its first one million tonnes of sugar in the current 1996/97 harvest, in which the island is hoping to improve on the 4.45 million tonnes it produced last season, a state newspaper said Friday.

Official Communist Party newspaper Granma said the first one million tonnes, reached Feb 10, was produced with less sugar cane than last year, which indicated some improvement in efficiency at the island's sugar mills.
It had taken 70 days of harvesting to achieve the current sugar total, the same time as that employed in 1995/96.
But at this time last year, 141 mills were grinding, whereas this year only 131 were in operation.
Cuba's 1996/97 sugar harvest has suffered delays because of the late arrival of essential spare parts and inputs like fertilizers, herbicides and pesticides.

Cuban officials have blamed these problems on disruptions to the flow of foreign financing for the Cuban sugar sector caused by the U.S. Helms-Burton legislation, which seeks to curb foreign investment in the Communist-ruled island.

This, and doubts about the availability and quality of sugar cane reserves this season, led the Cuban government to predict only a "modest" increase in the current crop over the 4.45 million tonnes produced last year with the help of foreign financing from mostly European banks and trade houses.
The past 1995/96 harvest was hailed as a success because it achieved an improvement of more than one million tonnes over the record low 1994/95 crop of 3.3 million tonnes.
Granma said the eastern provinces of Granma, Santiago de Cuba and Holguin had contributed most to this year's first million tonnes of sugar.
But other provinces are reported to be behind schedule in their harvesting because of slow supplies of cane to mills and operational hitches caused by the shortages of spare parts.

The government has made clear it needs every grain of sugar it can produce to meet international delivery commitments which in turn serve as guarantees to foreign credits granted to Cuba. Diplomats said they understood the Cuban sugar crop was heavily committed in this way, possibly for up to two years.
